title: Reuters Handbook of Journalism — Sourcing and the Essentials of Reuters Sourcing

extracted.subtask_short: Grading source strength and cross-checking wire claims
extracted.subtask_description: Judging whether a sourced statement in a wire story meets Reuters' sourcing bar — named vs. anonymous, single- vs. multi-source, rank of unnamed-source authority — before it can run as a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named source preferred; never mislead in sourcing
rubrics_metrics.description: A named source is always preferable to an unnamed source. Reuters should never deliberately mislead in sourcing, quote a source saying one thing on the record and something contradictory on background, or cite sources in the plural when only one exists. Anonymous sources are the weakest sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check information; weigh unnamed source's track record and motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-check information wherever possible: two or more sources are better than one. In assessing unnamed-source information, weigh the source's track record, position and motive. Talk to sources on all sides of a deal, dispute, negotiation or conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give context/detail about sources to enable authentication
rubrics_metrics.description: Give as much context and detail as possible about sources — named or anonymous — to let the information be authenticated. Be explicit about what is not known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single anonymous source only in exceptional, authorized cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuters will publish news from a single, anonymous source only in exceptional cases, when it is credible information from a trusted source with direct knowledge of the situation; single-source stories require special authorisation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source placed before claim for contentious/inflammatory statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statement in every story must be sourced unless it is an established fact or clearly in the public domain or the reporter/photographer witnessed it directly. A contentious statement must be sourced every time it appears — qualifying it with "alleged" is not protection against defamation. If a story is inflammatory or an allegation, the source is given before the claim (e.g., "X accused Y of..." not "Y did...").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to source every story within the first two paragraphs; stories of great importance should be sourced in the first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Named source still requires checking and balancing
rubrics_metrics.description: A named source doesn't remove responsibility for what is quoted — even named-source information should normally be checked and balanced, especially in conflict or negotiation. Naming gives more protection if a story is challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnamed-source strength ranking: authoritative > official > designated
rubrics_metrics.description: Unnamed sources must have direct knowledge of the information, or represent an authority with direct knowledge; reliability declines the further the source is from the event. Vague descriptions ("a source," "sources," "observers," "informed sources," "reliable sources") are unacceptable — specificity is required. Unnamed sources rank, in order of strength: authoritative source (real authority on the specific issue) > official source (access in an official capacity, limited to their field) > designated source (e.g., diplomatic, conference, intelligence sources with access to reliable information on the topic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories based on anonymous sources require particularly rigorous cross-checking — normally two or three sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-source story approval requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-source stories must be the exception and require approval by an immediate supervisor (bureau chief, unit head, or editor in charge), who must be satisfied the source is authoritative. For a single-source story, the informant must be an actual policymaker or participant with first-hand knowledge, or an official spokesperson speaking on background — subject to particular scrutiny against manipulation. Supervisor approval is noted on the outgoing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in sourcing — no pseudonyms, no false plurals
rubrics_metrics.description: Never use pseudonyms. Never cite sources in the plural when there is only one. Do not quote a source as declining comment if that same source gave information off the record; if on-record comment is still needed, seek it from another individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh every source's motive against other evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Every source has a motive; identify it and weigh it against other evidence. Two sources are always better than one — seek at least one from each side of a dispute. Give greatest weight to sources with a track record of accurate, unmisleading information. Try to disprove as well as prove a story; consult independent third parties to gauge reliability (e.g., a banker not involved in a deal, a think-tank analyst).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegations require on-record attribution, not anonymous cover
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources cannot make allegations or vituperative attacks behind a cloak of anonymity. Unnamed sources from one side of a conflict may be quoted only on facts, not opinions, about the other side. A source wanting to attack an individual, organization or country must speak on the record, unless a senior official is making a considered, clearly newsworthy policy statement — and the story must state both that the informant volunteered the information and that they are an official.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rumour-reporting procedure requiring two-source confirmation of the rumour itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Normal procedure for reporting rumours: (1) confirm from at least two sources what the rumour actually is, without spreading it; (2) attempt to determine whether it is true; (3) write a report noting that comment was sought (and whether it was obtained), and that checking continues. In fast-moving exceptional circumstances: have a second reporter check the rumour while the story is written; keep the description of the rumour vague so as not to lend it credibility; state explicitly that Reuters is checking; if confirmed or denied, issue a follow-up at equal priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never write of "unconfirmed rumours" as if that phrase makes them reportable — a rumour is by definition unconfirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickups require naming the originating source and independent confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickups must always name the originating source (newspaper, website, broadcaster, rival agency); using someone else's report does not exonerate Reuters from responsibility for accuracy, balance and legal soundness. Reporters must make every effort to independently check a pickup; if confirmation is not possible, the story must say so explicitly. Reuters must not rely on secondhand accounts of another outlet's report — it must see, hear or read the original report itself before running a story about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use "reports" or "unconfirmed reports" as the basis for a story on their own — quote an acceptable source commenting on them instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media/UGC verification against sleeper accounts and misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Twitter and similar sites are not sources in themselves. Verification of social-media material is a major issue: content might not be what it purports to be, due to sloppy posting or deliberate deceit. Checks include confirming an account is official (e.g., cross-referencing with other reputable coverage) and watching for "sleeper" or "shadow" accounts designed to spread misinformation. If a claim cannot be verified, Reuters may report only that the claim was posted, note what is/isn't known, and continue trying to confirm or knock it down independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any residual uncertainty about provenance must be made explicit to the reader.
